 England beware: Wounded All Blacks are bloodthirsty for revenge
 Borthwick’s side should be braced for a rejuvenated New Zealand desperate to restore pride in famous old jersey after Wales humiliation

 Rugby Reporter
 Show biography 
 Based a stone's throw from the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham, Charles has worked for the Telegraph since 2019 and was heavily involved in coverage for both the 2021 Lions tour of South Africa and the 2023 men's World Cup in France. You can find him @CharlesRTel on X.
 Published 
 20 November 2026 10:00am GMT
 Dave Rennie was asked this week whether, in New Zealand’s against-the-odds defeat by Wales last Saturday, the All Blacks jersey had hung heavy on his players’ shoulders.
 With 73 years of history to protect – and that was just against Wales – had the All Blacks been burdened by pressure? Were they hamstrung by the persistent expectation of a nation accustomed to nothing but victory, and by a desperation to do justice to what had been left behind by some of rugby’s greatest players?
 “We never use the word burden but we talk a lot about legacy and building on it,” Rennie, the New Zealand head coach, said. “We took a step backwards last weekend. It’s important that we respond and try to add to the jersey.”
 The All Blacks jersey is a funny old thing; simultaneously the most recognisable and, more often than not, the most revered in global rugby. It is the only jersey in the sport – perhaps, arguably, any sport – where its “aura” is mentioned as often as the ability of those wearing it. The All Blacks jersey has carried an abstract, intangible quality; almost as if some of the great players who have worn it, in times of adversity, have been able to summon a supernatural spirit to turn tides and find a path to victory.
 Last year, however, there was a feeling among the Twickenham faithful such an aura might be on the wane. England finished as, ultimately, comfortable 33-19 winners against New Zealand , a team they had only previously beaten eight times out of 46. England that day had as their midfield combination Fraser Dingwall, an unused member of the current squad, and Ollie Lawrence, currently a way down the Test pecking order, yet still ran out 14-point victors. Some believed it might have been the worst All Blacks side that they had seen in south-west London.
 Scott Robertson (right) was sacked as All Blacks head coach two months after defeat at Twickenham
 Credit : Getty Images/David Rogers
 A year is a long time in sport and on Saturday, a totally different All Blacks proposition will arrive at Twickenham. Rennie’s side are depleted, missing nearly half of a first-choice starting XV, but since the coach took over from Scott Robertson there is renewed optimism. Notwithstanding the defeat by Wales – there has been soul-searching this week and the side that New Zealand picked were still eminently good enough to win, but it was still a de facto second string – it has started to look as though the All Blacks have got their mojo back.
 Certainly, there has been little to suggest that England have been complacent this week. Rennie might have bristled at the suggestion last weekend’s defeat in Cardiff was irrelevant to proceedings at Twickenham this Saturday, given the differences in both selection and challenge, but that is certainly the prevailing attitude within the England camp. This is England against a developing New Zealand side which, until last Saturday, had been very much on the up. It is England against the All Blacks for, perhaps, a spot in a Twickenham final. Victory would be a scalp.
 “They’ve got 500 caps coming back in, a different team, a different game,” Richard Wigglesworth, England’s senior assistant coach, said. “In Cardiff, they had a world-record amount of rucks and it was the fewest times they’d kicked; I don’t see that [this Saturday].
 “What happened last weekend definitely has nothing to do with how big this fixture is. It’s England versus New Zealand. It’s historic; it feels like it always will be. Whether there’s any extra edge in training... there’s a keenness that we always see from our lads, to get out there and rip in.”
 New Zealand lost to Wales for the first time since 1953
 Credit : AFP/Adrian Dennis
 Emotionally, England know this weekend’s meeting will be a more significant challenge than the equivalent fixture last year. Tactically, too, they have been preparing for a much changed All Blacks approach.
 “They’ve changed a fair bit,” Wigglesworth said. “They’ve talked pretty openly about playing more ‘New Zealand’ rugby, which has resulted in significantly more phases, ball movement.
 “We’re expecting them to kick a little bit more than they did last week. They have gone from not factoring in that contestable part of the game in terms of our [rankings], to being one of the very, very best. That will be around [scrum-half] Cam Roigard’s left boot – accurate – and the two centres but, particularly, Jordie Barrett coming on the inside, taking clean catches, launching their attack. That’s going to be a key battleground ground again.”
 Jordie Barrett, the New Zealand centre, returns to the fold having sat out the defeat in Cardiff
 Credit : Getty Images/Dan Mullan
 In terms of metrics, taking last weekend’s defeat as an aberration, New Zealand are above their 2025 average in several notable attacking areas, and that is with having played South Africa, the reigning world champions, four times already this year.
 The percentage of plays that the All Blacks play wider than the first receiver is up and handling errors are down. As well as Wigglesworth’s remark that they have increased their phase count and their contestable kicking, they are also moving the ball swifter, wider and more accurately. Their percentage of line breaks leading to tries is up two percentage points and their tackle evasion rate is up, too. New Zealand are shrewdly identifying space, efficiently putting team-mates into it, and busting a gut to support them.
 These All Blacks are more ruthless, too. Even with that Springboks caveat, their rate of points per attacking 22 entry is up from 3.3 to almost four, on average, while the number of possessions, or phases, required to score has almost halved, from 11 to 6.9. This has all meant that the number of tries they score on average per match has increased from four in 2025 to 5.6 this year.
 This weekend, at Twickenham, they will need that. The New Zealand Herald reports that the All Blacks have not managed four tries against England in the last 10 meetings between the two sides – admittedly, bonus points are seldom in play in these matches – but on Saturday the visitors require a quartet of scores to guarantee top spot in the southern hemisphere table.
 England know what is coming. A rejuvenated-yet-wounded set of All Blacks. Under the circumstances – a lethal team bloodthirsty for revenge, playing for the legacy of themselves and the jersey – any victory must be savoured.
